Proposed Method: We introduce Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping (CGRS), which augments verifiable task rewards with an explicit diversity bonus that incentivizes generating reasoning trajectories not already covered by the base model's distribution. Specifically, we maintain a solution fingerprint library (via clustering of reasoning chain embeddings) and reward solutions that occupy novel regions of the base model's low-probability space. We combine this with a KL penalty against the base model to push exploration into underrepresented reasoning strategies, effectively transforming RLVR from mode-seeking to mode-expanding. Experiments: We evaluate CGRS on MATH, AIME, HumanEval, and visual reasoning benchmarks across Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3 families. Primary metrics are pass@k curves across k=1 to k=256, solution cluster diversity, and a novel 'coverage expansion ratio' measuring how much CGRS-trained models exceed base model coverage. We compare against six RLVR baselines from the anchor paper and distillation as a reference ceiling, hypothesizing CGRS can partially bridge the gap between RLVR and distillation in genuine capability expansion.

title: Escape Velocity: Measuring and Inducing Reasoning Patterns That Transcend Base Model Coverage via Iterative Distillation-RL Hybrid Training
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR merely reshapes the distribution of base model reasoning without generating genuinely novel patterns. Yet distillation can introduce new capabilities. This raises a critical question: can we design a training paradigm that systematically expands reasoning coverage beyond both the base model and a fixed teacher? Proposed Method: We introduce an iterative Distillation-then-RLVR loop. In each cycle, (1) a stronger teacher model generates solutions the student base model cannot produce (measured via pass@k coverage gaps), (2) the student is distilled on these 'coverage-expanding' solutions, and (3) RLVR is applied to consolidate and stabilize the new capabilities. We introduce a metric called Reasoning Escape Rate (RER): the fraction of problems where the trained model succeeds at k=1 but the original base model fails even at large k, directly quantifying genuinely novel reasoning acquisition. We also study whether successive cycles compound reasoning gains or saturate. Experiments: We apply this on Qwen2.5-7B/14B and LLaMA-3.1-8B across MATH500, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning benchmarks, comparing against standalone RLVR, pure distillation, and self-play baselines, measuring RER, pass@k curves, and reasoning diversity via solution clustering.

title: Escaping the Base Model Ceiling: Iterative Distillation-RL Cycles for Genuinely Novel Reasoning Acquisition
description:
Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR is bounded by the base model's latent reasoning capacity—it cannot generate genuinely new reasoning patterns. However, distillation can introduce novel capabilities from a teacher. This raises a key question: can we design an iterative pipeline where distillation and RLVR alternate to progressively expand reasoning boundaries beyond any single base model's ceiling?

Proposed Method: We introduce Distill-RL Bootstrapping (DRB), an iterative curriculum where: (1) a stronger teacher model generates high-quality reasoning traces for hard problems the student consistently fails (pass@k ≈ 0 for large k); (2) distillation fine-tuning injects these novel patterns into the student, raising its reasoning ceiling; (3) RLVR then consolidates and improves sampling efficiency on the expanded capability set; (4) the updated model becomes the new baseline, and the cycle repeats. Each iteration targets problems at the frontier of the current model's coverage boundary.

Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning benchmarks using pass@k metrics (k=1,16,64,256) across iterations. We track coverage expansion, perplexity of novel solutions, and compare against pure RLVR, pure distillation, and single-cycle baselines. We measure whether each DRB iteration genuinely raises the pass@k ceiling beyond the initial base model, quantifying compounding capability gains across 3-5 cycles.

title: Hybrid Distillation-RLVR: Expanding the Reasoning Frontier by Bootstrapping Base Model Coverage
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR is bounded by base model coverage (pass@k ceiling) while distillation genuinely expands reasoning patterns. This raises a critical question: can we combine distillation's coverage expansion with RLVR's precision sharpening to surpass both individually? Proposed Method: We propose a two-phase hybrid training pipeline. Phase 1 (Coverage Expansion): Perform targeted distillation from a stronger teacher model, but selectively distill only on problem instances where the base model has zero pass@k coverage (i.e., genuinely out-of-distribution reasoning patterns the base cannot solve even with large k). This creates an expanded-coverage student. Phase 2 (Precision Sharpening): Apply RLVR on top of this distilled student, now operating over a genuinely enlarged reasoning space. We hypothesize RLVR can then improve pass@1 performance within the newly expanded coverage without reverting to original base model boundaries. We also introduce an adaptive curriculum that routes easy problems to RLVR and hard zero-coverage problems to distillation dynamically. Experiments: Evaluate on MATH, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning benchmarks using pass@k (k=1,4,16,64,256) to measure both coverage expansion and precision. Ablate phase ordering, distillation volume, and curriculum strategies across Qwen2.5 and LLaMA3 model families.

title: Reasoning Boundary Expansion via Iterative Distillation-RL Cycles: Breaking the Base Model Ceiling
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR is bounded by the base model's reasoning coverage—it refines selection but cannot generate genuinely novel reasoning patterns. Distillation can expand this boundary by injecting teacher knowledge. However, distillation introduces a static ceiling from the teacher model. We propose an iterative framework that alternates distillation and RLVR to progressively expand reasoning boundaries beyond any single teacher. Method: Starting from a base model, we (1) distill from a stronger teacher to inject novel reasoning patterns, expanding the base coverage ceiling; (2) apply RLVR to improve selection efficiency within the expanded space; (3) use the fine-tuned model as a new 'pseudo-teacher' for self-distillation augmented with diverse solution sampling; and (4) repeat. The key insight is that each distillation step raises the coverage ceiling, while each RLVR step improves precision, creating a compounding effect. We introduce a 'reasoning novelty score' measuring the fraction of correct solutions at large k that were absent before each cycle. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning benchmarks using pass@k (k=1,10,100) across cycles, comparing against standalone RLVR, standalone distillation, and concurrent distillation+RL baselines with Qwen2.5 and DeepSeek model families.

title: Hybrid Distillation-RLVR: Expanding Reasoning Coverage Before Reinforcement Fine-Tuning
description:
Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR is bounded by base model coverage—it cannot elicit reasoning patterns absent from the base model, while distillation genuinely expands coverage. However, distillation alone lacks the selective pressure to improve precision at k=1. This creates a natural question: can sequentially combining distillation and RLVR yield models that both expand reasoning coverage (high pass@large-k) and improve precision (high pass@k=1)?

Proposed Method: We propose a two-stage training pipeline—(1) Targeted Coverage Distillation (TCD): distill from a stronger teacher specifically on problems where the base model has zero coverage (pass@128 = 0), expanding the model's reasoning frontier; (2) RLVR Precision Amplification: apply RLVR starting from the distilled checkpoint to convert expanded coverage into reliable first-shot performance. We introduce a 'coverage-gain score' to select distillation examples maximally orthogonal to base model solutions.

Experiments: We evaluate on MATH500, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and MathVista using pass@k for k∈{1,4,16,64,256}. Baselines: base model, RLVR-only, distillation-only, naive distillation+RLVR. We measure coverage expansion, precision at k=1, and perplexity over novel solution patterns. Ablations vary distillation data selection strategies and ordering of stages. We test across Qwen-2.5 and DeepSeek-R1 model families.

title: Reasoning Boundary Expansion via Iterative Distillation-RL Cycles: Escaping the Base Model Ceiling
description:
Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR is bounded by the base model's latent reasoning capacity, while distillation genuinely expands capabilities. This raises a critical question: can we systematically combine distillation and RL in iterative cycles to progressively expand the reasoning frontier beyond any single base model's ceiling?

Proposed Method: We introduce Iterative Distillation-RL (IDRL), a bootstrapping paradigm that alternates between two phases: (1) Distillation Phase — use a stronger teacher (e.g., GPT-4o or DeepSeek-R1) to inject novel reasoning patterns into the current student model via chain-of-thought distillation on problems the student cannot solve; (2) RL Consolidation Phase — apply RLVR to consolidate and refine the newly distilled patterns, improving reliability at small-k. The key insight is that each distillation phase raises the capability ceiling, while RL then efficiently exploits the expanded space. We use pass@k across multiple k values as the primary diagnostic to verify that each cycle genuinely expands coverage beyond the previous iteration's ceiling.

Experiments: We evaluate IDRL on MATH-500, AIME, HumanEval+, and LiveCodeBench across 7B and 14B model families. Ablations compare: RL-only, distillation-only, simultaneous mixing, and IDRL cycles. We measure pass@k for k∈{1,4,16,64,256} to verify genuine boundary expansion across cycles, demonstrating escape from the single-base-model ceiling.

title: Escaping the Base Model Ceiling: Curiosity-Driven Exploration in RLVR to Generate Out-of-Distribution Reasoning Traces
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR merely reweights reasoning patterns already present in the base model, never exceeding its pass@k coverage ceiling. The core failure is insufficient exploration—standard RLVR with correctness-only rewards collapses toward high-probability base model solutions rather than discovering genuinely novel reasoning paths. Proposed Method: We introduce Curiosity-Augmented RLVR (CA-RLVR), which supplements the verifiable correctness reward with an intrinsic curiosity bonus measuring how much a generated reasoning trace deviates from the base model's distribution. Specifically, we compute the KL divergence between the trace and the base model's predictive distribution token-by-token, rewarding traces that are simultaneously correct AND low-probability under the base model. We additionally incorporate a diversity regularizer across rollouts within a batch to prevent mode collapse to a single novel path. Experiments: (1) We replicate the pass@k coverage analysis from the anchor paper, comparing CA-RLVR against standard GRPO/PPO across Qwen-2.5 and DeepSeek model families on MATH500, LiveCodeBench, and OlympiadBench. (2) We measure whether CA-RLVR genuinely raises the pass@k ceiling beyond the base model at large k. (3) We perform perplexity and clustering analysis of generated traces to verify structural novelty. (4) We ablate the curiosity reward weight and diversity regularizer. Success criterion: CA-RLVR achieves pass@k > base model at k≥64 on at least two benchmarks.

title: Reasoning Boundary Expansion via Iterative Distillation-RL Cycles: Escaping the Base Model Ceiling
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR is bounded by base model reasoning capacity, while distillation genuinely expands capabilities. This raises an actionable question: can we systematically escape the base model ceiling by alternating distillation and RL phases in iterative cycles, using each RL phase to consolidate and sharpen distilled patterns before the next distillation round expands them further? Proposed Method: We introduce Iterative Distillation-RL (IDRL), a training paradigm where: (1) distillation from a stronger teacher injects novel reasoning patterns into the student, (2) RLVR consolidates and improves the reliability of these patterns (improving pass@1 without shrinking coverage), then (3) the refined model acts as an improved student for the next distillation round, potentially bootstrapping from a synthetic teacher generated via majority voting over its own expanded coverage. We track pass@k curves across cycles to verify ceiling-lifting versus mere sharpening. Experiments: We train Qwen2.5-7B and LLaMA-3-8B through 3-4 IDRL cycles on MATH, AIME, and LiveCodeBench, measuring pass@k (k=1,4,16,64,256), coverage, and perplexity of novel solutions at each cycle. Ablations isolate distillation-only, RL-only, and joint schedules. We hypothesize IDRL progressively raises the effective reasoning ceiling measurably above the original base model.

title: Boundary-Aware RLVR: Dynamically Expanding Base Model Coverage Through Targeted Exploration Bonuses
description: Problem: The anchor paper reveals that RLVR merely redistributes probability mass within the base model's existing reasoning patterns rather than discovering genuinely novel solutions. The key bottleneck is that standard RL reward signals only reinforce correct answers, providing no incentive to explore reasoning trajectories outside the base model's high-probability regions. Method: We propose Boundary-Aware RLVR (BA-RLVR), which augments standard verifiable rewards with an explicit coverage expansion bonus. Concretely, we maintain a trajectory diversity buffer tracking the semantic clustering of successful reasoning chains. At each training step, we compute a novelty score measuring how far a newly discovered correct trajectory lies from previously seen solution clusters (using embedding-based distance metrics). This novelty score is added as an auxiliary reward, incentivizing the policy to find correct solutions via underexplored reasoning paths. To prevent reward hacking, novelty bonuses decay as clusters become populated. We additionally incorporate base model perplexity thresholds to specifically target low-probability but correct trajectories. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, GSM8K, and coding benchmarks measuring pass@k across k=1 to k=200, comparing BA-RLVR against standard GRPO/PPO baselines and distillation. Primary metrics include coverage expansion relative to the base model, pass@1 vs. pass@100 tradeoffs, and solution cluster diversity. We hypothesize BA-RLVR will genuinely expand beyond base model boundaries while maintaining competitive greedy performance.

title: Escape Velocity: Training RLVR Models to Exceed Base Model Coverage via Curiosity-Driven Exploration Bonuses
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR-trained LLMs never exceed base model pass@k at large k, meaning RL only reshapes the sampling distribution without generating genuinely novel reasoning trajectories. This bottleneck stems from RL's exploitation of already-probable base model outputs rather than exploring low-probability but correct reasoning chains. Proposed Method: We augment standard RLVR with a curiosity-driven exploration bonus that rewards solutions residing in low-probability regions of the base model's distribution. Concretely, we compute a novelty score for each generated trajectory as the negative log-probability under the frozen base model, then add a weighted novelty bonus to the verifiable reward signal. To prevent reward hacking (generating gibberish that is merely unlikely), we pair this with a semantic coherence filter using embedding-based similarity to correct reference solutions. We also incorporate a diversity penalty discouraging redundant novel trajectories within a training batch. Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate pass@k (k up to 256) on MATH, AIME, and HumanEval comparing baseline RLVR, our curiosity-augmented RLVR, and distillation; (2) Coverage analysis measuring how much of the base model's solution space is accessed vs. newly discovered; (3) Perplexity-stratified accuracy to confirm gains come from genuinely low-probability regions; (4) Ablations on novelty bonus weight and coherence thresholds across Qwen2.5 and Llama3 model families.

title: Escape Velocity: Using Entropy-Regularized RL to Expand the Reasoning Boundary Beyond Base Model Coverage
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR is bounded by base model coverage—it improves selection efficiency (low k) but never generates reasoning patterns absent from the base model (high k). This suggests current RLVR exploits existing latent solutions rather than discovering novel ones. We hypothesize that standard reward-maximizing RL collapses output diversity, while an entropy-augmented objective could force exploration into genuinely novel reasoning trajectories outside base model support. Method: We propose Coverage-Expanding RL (CERL), which augments the standard verifiable reward with (1) a novelty bonus measuring cosine distance of generated reasoning chains from base model high-probability trajectories, and (2) a maximum-entropy regularizer penalizing premature token-level certainty. We implement CERL on top of GRPO and PPO, training Qwen-2.5-Math and DeepSeek-R1-Distill on MATH and AMC benchmarks. Experiments: We evaluate using the anchor paper's pass@k framework (k up to 256) alongside our proposed 'new-coverage@k' metric—the fraction of correct solutions at large k that are absent from base model's top-10000 samples. We compare CERL against standard GRPO, PPO, and distillation baselines. Ablations isolate contributions of novelty bonus vs. entropy regularization. Success means CERL's new-coverage@k exceeds base model coverage, demonstrating genuine reasoning boundary expansion.

title: Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping: Expanding Base Model Reasoning Boundaries via Diversity-Incentivized RLVR
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR merely sharpens the probability of reasoning paths already latent in the base model without expanding coverage—the base model's pass@k at large k upper-bounds RLVR-trained models. This means standard verifiable reward signals (correct/incorrect) implicitly encourage mode-seeking, collapsing reasoning diversity rather than expanding it. Proposed Method: We introduce Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping (CGRS), which augments verifiable correctness rewards with an explicit diversity bonus computed online. At each training step, we maintain a rolling sketch of solution trajectories (via semantic embedding clustering or n-gram hashing) and reward solutions that are both correct AND structurally distinct from previously seen correct solutions. This creates pressure to discover novel reasoning chains rather than reinforce dominant ones. We further propose a 'coverage temperature curriculum' that gradually increases diversity pressure as training progresses, preventing early instability. Planned Experiments: (1) Compare pass@k (k=1,10,100) curves of CGRS vs. standard GRPO/PPO/REINFORCE on MATH500, AIME, and HumanEval across Qwen2.5-7B and DeepSeek-R1-distill families; (2) Measure whether CGRS-trained models exceed base model pass@k ceilings identified in the anchor paper; (3) Ablate diversity bonus weight, sketch size, and curriculum schedule; (4) Analyze whether new solution clusters emerge that were zero-probability under base model sampling.

title: Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping: Expanding Base Model Reasoning Boundaries Through Exploration Bonuses in RLVR
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR merely reshuffles base model probability mass toward correct solutions (improving pass@1) without genuinely expanding the solution space (pass@k ceiling equals base model). This means RLVR wastes potential by over-exploiting already-discovered reasoning patterns rather than exploring novel ones latent in the base model. Proposed Method: We introduce Coverage-Guided RLVR (CG-RLVR), which augments standard verifiable reward signals with an intrinsic exploration bonus that incentivizes structural diversity in reasoning traces. Specifically, we maintain a rolling buffer of solution sketches (abstracted proof/computation graphs) per problem and reward generations that introduce novel graph structures not yet observed. The bonus decays as coverage saturates, preventing reward hacking. We combine this with a pass@k-aware training objective that explicitly optimizes for coverage at moderate k values (k=8,16) rather than greedy accuracy. Experiments: We train on MATH, GSM8K, and MBPP using Qwen-2.5 and DeepSeek-R1-Zero base models. Evaluation measures pass@k curves (k=1 to 100), solution diversity via edit distance and structural clustering, and perplexity on novel reasoning chains. We compare against six RLVR baselines from the anchor paper. Success criterion: CG-RLVR narrows the pass@k gap between RLVR and base model at large k, demonstrating genuine reasoning boundary expansion.

title: Distillation-Bootstrapped RLVR: Using Teacher-Expanded Coverage to Break Base Model Ceilings
description:
Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR is bounded by the base model's reasoning coverage (pass@k ceiling), while distillation genuinely expands capabilities by introducing novel reasoning patterns from a teacher. Yet distillation alone lacks the selectivity and efficiency of RL. Can we combine both—using distillation to break the base model ceiling, then applying RLVR to consolidate and refine the expanded reasoning space?

Proposed Method: We introduce a two-phase training pipeline. Phase 1 (Coverage Expansion): Perform a targeted distillation step using only teacher solutions that lie outside the base model's existing coverage—identified by filtering for problems where the base model fails at large k but the teacher succeeds. This specifically injects novel reasoning patterns. Phase 2 (RLVR Consolidation): Apply RLVR starting from the distillation-expanded model, now with a higher ceiling, to improve pass@1 reliability across the expanded reasoning space. We also introduce a 'coverage delta' metric to track how much each phase shifts the pass@k curve.

Experiments: Evaluate on MATH, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning (MathVista) using pass@k for k∈{1,4,16,64,256}. Ablations isolate contribution of each phase. Compare against RLVR-only, distillation-only, and naive sequential baselines across Qwen-2.5, Llama-3, and DeepSeek model families.

title: Escape Velocity: Using Distillation-Seeded Exploration to Break the Base Model Ceiling in RLVR
description:
Problem: The anchor paper shows that RLVR is bounded by the base model's reasoning coverage—it selects and sharpens existing patterns but never introduces genuinely novel ones. Distillation can exceed this ceiling by importing new reasoning patterns from a teacher. Can we combine both advantages: distillation's ability to introduce novel patterns with RL's ability to optimize for verifiable rewards?

Method: We propose a three-phase training pipeline called Distillation-Seeded RL (DSRL). Phase 1: Standard SFT distillation from a stronger teacher on a small curated set, deliberately targeting problem types where the base model has near-zero pass@k coverage. Phase 2: RLVR fine-tuning initialized from the distilled checkpoint, using a curriculum that progressively focuses on problems where the distilled model still fails. Phase 3: A diversity-promoting reward term penalizing solution-path similarity (measured via edit distance on chain-of-thought traces) alongside correctness rewards, explicitly incentivizing exploration beyond distilled patterns.

Experiments: Evaluate on MATH, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and a new held-out 'boundary problems' suite (problems with zero base model pass@512). Key metrics: pass@k for k∈{1,8,64,512}, solution diversity entropy, and coverage delta over base model. Ablations isolate each phase's contribution and compare against distillation-only and RLVR-only baselines across Qwen2.5 and LLaMA-3 families.

title: Escape Velocity: Measuring and Inducing Out-of-Coverage Reasoning in LLMs via Curiosity-Driven Exploration with Verifiable Rewards
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR is bounded by base model coverage—it refines selection over existing reasoning patterns rather than generating genuinely novel ones. We ask: can modified RL training signals actively push models to produce reasoning trajectories that lie outside the base model's coverage, and how do we measure this rigorously? Proposed Method: We introduce a 'novelty bonus' reward shaping scheme inspired by curiosity-driven RL: alongside the standard verifiable correctness reward, we add a bonus for solutions whose token-level perplexity under the frozen base model exceeds a threshold, incentivizing exploration of low-probability (novel) reasoning chains. We call this Coverage-Escaping RLVR (CE-RLVR). To prevent reward hacking toward incoherent high-perplexity outputs, we add a fluency/coherence constraint via a lightweight discriminator. Experiments: (1) We train CE-RLVR on Qwen-2.5 and DeepSeek-R1-Zero family models on MATH, AIME, and ARC-AGI benchmarks. (2) We evaluate pass@k for k∈{1,4,16,64,256} comparing base, standard RLVR, distillation, and CE-RLVR. (3) We measure coverage expansion via embedding-space diversity of generated solutions and clustering analyses. (4) We ablate novelty bonus weight and perplexity threshold to characterize the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. Expected contribution: First demonstration that explicit novelty incentives in RLVR can meaningfully expand the base model's reasoning coverage, providing a path toward genuinely novel reasoning abilities.

title: Beyond Coverage Ceilings: Iterative Self-Distillation with RLVR to Genuinely Expand LLM Reasoning Boundaries
description:
Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR is bounded by the base model's existing reasoning coverage (pass@k ceiling), while distillation genuinely expands capabilities by introducing teacher patterns. However, distillation requires a stronger external teacher, creating a dependency bottleneck. Can we design a self-improving loop that combines RLVR's reinforcement signal with distillation-like expansion to break the base model's coverage ceiling without requiring an external teacher?

Proposed Method: We propose Iterative Self-Distillation via Reward-Guided Exploration (ISRE). In each iteration: (1) Run RLVR training to improve pass@1 reliability; (2) Use the trained model to generate a large pool of solutions (high-k sampling), selecting novel correct solutions that were NOT producible by the base model (verified via base model perplexity thresholding); (3) Distill these genuinely new solutions back as supervised fine-tuning targets for the next iteration's base; (4) Repeat, effectively using the RLVR model's explorations to bootstrap new reasoning patterns into the next-generation base model.

Experiments: Measure pass@k (k=1 to 256) across iterations on MATH, AIME, and LiveCodeBench. Track coverage expansion relative to original base model. Compare against vanilla RLVR, standard distillation from GPT-4o, and standard self-play. Ablate perplexity threshold for novelty filtering. Primary metric: whether successive iterations genuinely raise the pass@k ceiling beyond the original base model.

title: Beyond Base Model Boundaries: Expanding LLM Reasoning via Environment-Grounded Multi-Turn RL
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR merely redistributes probability mass within the base model's existing reasoning patterns rather than discovering genuinely novel ones. We hypothesize this limitation stems from single-turn, outcome-only reward signals that prevent models from encountering reasoning states outside their prior distribution. Proposed Method: We design a multi-turn agent-environment RL framework where LLMs interact with executable sandboxes (Python interpreters, formal proof assistants like Lean 4) across iterative refinement steps. Critically, we augment the reward signal with dense, step-level 'novelty bonuses' computed as inverse perplexity under the base model—explicitly incentivizing the policy to traverse low-probability reasoning trajectories. We further introduce 'boundary injection': when the agent stalls in high-perplexity regions, a retrieval mechanism seeds partial solutions from a distillation corpus, bootstrapping exploration beyond the base distribution. Experiments: (1) We replicate the anchor paper's pass@k evaluation framework on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench, and MiniF2F to establish baselines. (2) We compare our method against six RLVR algorithms from the anchor paper using coverage and perplexity metrics. (3) We quantify how often our trained models produce correct solutions with perplexity exceeding the base model's 95th percentile—our primary metric for 'genuinely novel reasoning.' We target 3B and 7B model families to assess scaling behavior.

title: Distillation-Bootstrapped RLVR: Using Teacher-Expanded Reasoning Boundaries as Exploration Targets for Reinforcement Learning
description:
Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR cannot exceed base model reasoning boundaries (measured by pass@k), while distillation genuinely expands them by introducing novel reasoning patterns from a teacher. This creates a natural question: can distillation be used not as an end goal but as a bootstrapping mechanism to create better exploration targets for subsequent RLVR training, potentially enabling RL to surpass both the original base model and pure distillation?

Proposed Method: We propose a two-phase pipeline. Phase 1: Apply distillation from a stronger teacher model to expand the student's reasoning coverage, creating a 'distilled base' with genuinely new reasoning patterns. Phase 2: Apply RLVR on top of this distilled base, hypothesizing that the expanded reasoning distribution now provides richer exploration trajectories for RL to select and reinforce high-reward behaviors. We additionally introduce a 'boundary-aware' reward shaping that explicitly rewards solutions falling outside the original base model's high-probability regions (measured via perplexity), incentivizing exploration of the newly acquired reasoning patterns.

Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, AIME, and HumanEval benchmarks across Qwen and LLaMA families, measuring pass@k for k∈{1,4,16,64,256}, coverage, and perplexity distributions. Ablations compare: base→RLVR, base→distill, base→distill→RLVR, and base→distill→boundary-aware-RLVR.

title: Coverage-Guided Exploration Bonuses for RLVR: Incentivizing Novel Reasoning Trajectories Beyond Base Model Boundaries
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR-trained models fail to generate reasoning patterns not already latent in the base model, with base model pass@k at large k forming a hard ceiling. This suggests current RLVR reward signals (correctness only) provide no incentive to explore genuinely novel solution trajectories, causing RL to merely sharpen existing high-probability paths rather than discover new ones. Proposed Method: We introduce Coverage-Guided RLVR (CG-RLVR), augmenting the standard verifiable reward with an intrinsic exploration bonus that rewards reasoning trajectories whose token-level or step-level representations are novel relative to a maintained buffer of previously seen solution paths. Concretely, we embed chain-of-thought reasoning steps using a lightweight frozen encoder and compute novelty as distance to a nearest-neighbor buffer. This novelty bonus is annealed over training to balance exploration and exploitation. We also experiment with diversity-promoting constrained optimization that explicitly penalizes low-coverage solution sets. Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate pass@k for k in {1, 4, 16, 64, 256} on MATH, AIME, HumanEval, and LiveCodeBench to measure whether CG-RLVR expands the coverage ceiling beyond the base model. (2) Perplexity and clustering analyses to verify genuinely new reasoning patterns emerge. (3) Ablations on novelty buffer size, encoder choice, and annealing schedule. (4) Compare against distillation baselines to quantify the coverage gap.

title: Hybrid Distillation-RL: Using Teacher Coverage Gaps to Guide Reinforcement Learning Beyond Base Model Boundaries
description:
Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR is bounded by base model coverage while distillation genuinely expands reasoning capabilities by introducing novel patterns from a teacher. However, distillation alone suffers from teacher imitation without verification, potentially propagating teacher errors. Can we combine both paradigms to transcend both limitations?

Proposed Method: We propose Coverage-Guided Distillation-RL (CGDR), a two-phase hybrid training framework. Phase 1 performs targeted distillation specifically on problems where the base model has zero pass@k coverage (identified via large-k sampling), importing novel reasoning patterns from a stronger teacher exclusively for these 'coverage holes.' Phase 2 applies RLVR on problems where the base model already has non-zero coverage, using verifiable rewards to sharpen selection among known strategies. A coverage-aware curriculum dynamically balances distillation vs. RL training signal based on estimated problem-level base model coverage throughout training.

Experiments: We evaluate on MATH500, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning benchmarks using both pass@1 and pass@k (k up to 256). Ablations compare: (1) pure RLVR, (2) pure distillation, (3) naive RLVR+distillation mixture, (4) CGDR. Key metrics include coverage expansion beyond base model, pass@1 improvement, and novel reasoning pattern analysis via embedding-space clustering of generated solutions.

title: Escape Velocity: Curriculum-Based Multi-Turn RLVR with Adversarial Environment Feedback to Transcend Base Model Reasoning Boundaries
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that current RLVR methods merely reshape the probability distribution over reasoning paths already latent in the base model rather than discovering genuinely novel reasoning strategies. This raises a fundamental question: can carefully designed multi-turn agent-environment interactions push RLVR beyond the base model's coverage ceiling? Method: We propose CurriculumRL-Escape, a multi-turn RLVR framework where an LLM agent iteratively interacts with an adversarial problem-generation environment that dynamically synthesizes problems outside the current model's solution coverage. Specifically, we train a lightweight adversarial problem generator (APG) that identifies 'boundary problems'—problems where the base model's pass@large-k is nonzero but small—and incrementally increases difficulty, forcing the policy to construct reasoning chains not present in the base model's distribution. Verifiable rewards come from symbolic solvers. We augment standard PPO with a 'novelty bonus' penalizing solutions that closely match base model generation patterns (measured via embedding similarity). Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and novel geometry benchmarks using pass@k (k up to 256), coverage gap metrics, and perplexity analysis from the anchor paper. We compare against standard GRPO/PPO baselines and distillation, measuring whether coverage genuinely exceeds the base model ceiling across training epochs.

title: Distillation-Bootstrapped RLVR: Using Teacher-Expanded Coverage to Guide Reinforcement Learning Beyond Base Model Boundaries
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR is bounded by the base model's reasoning coverage, while distillation genuinely expands capabilities by introducing novel reasoning patterns from a teacher. However, distillation alone lacks the self-improvement dynamics of RL. This suggests a hybrid approach: use distillation to first expand the model's reasoning frontier, then apply RLVR to optimize within this expanded space. Method: We propose a two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 performs targeted distillation focused specifically on problem types where the base model has near-zero pass@k coverage (identified via systematic coverage profiling), injecting genuinely novel reasoning patterns from a stronger teacher. Stage 2 applies RLVR on this distillation-expanded model. We additionally propose a coverage-aware reward shaping scheme that gives bonus rewards for solutions that differ structurally from those already in the base model's distribution, measured via embedding-based diversity metrics. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning benchmarks across Qwen and Llama families. Key metrics include pass@k at various k values, coverage expansion curves, and perplexity analysis. We compare against RLVR-only, distillation-only, and naive sequential baselines to isolate the contribution of each stage and the coverage-aware reward signal.

title: Escape Velocity: Curriculum-Guided Exploration Bonuses to Break the Base Model Ceiling in RLVR
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR-trained LLMs are bounded by their base model's reasoning coverage—they improve pass@1 but cannot generate solutions the base model never produces, suggesting insufficient exploration of genuinely novel reasoning trajectories. Current RLVR methods essentially exploit existing base model capabilities rather than explore beyond them. Method: We propose RLVR-Explore, which augments standard verifiable reward RL with a novelty-driven exploration bonus. Concretely, we maintain a hash-based sketch of solution trajectories seen during training and add an intrinsic reward proportional to semantic distance from previously observed correct solutions (measured via embedding cosine distance). To prevent reward hacking, we apply a curriculum that phases in the exploration bonus only after baseline correctness is established, and cap bonuses for solutions that are novel but structurally incoherent. We additionally incorporate a small synthetic distillation signal from a stronger teacher on a held-out 5% of training data as an 'anchor' for genuinely new patterns. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH500, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and geometry visual reasoning, measuring pass@k for k∈{1,4,16,64,256} against base models and standard GRPO/PPO baselines. We track coverage expansion (new correct solutions vs. base model), perplexity of generated solutions, and performance on out-of-distribution problem variants to verify that newly discovered patterns genuinely generalize.

title: Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping: Expanding Base Model Reasoning Boundaries via Diversity-Incentivized RLVR
description:
Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR merely reshuffles probability mass within the base model's existing solution space rather than discovering genuinely novel reasoning patterns—base model pass@k at large k consistently upper-bounds RLVR-trained models. This suggests current reward signals optimize for greedy correctness (pass@1) while neglecting solution diversity, leaving vast latent reasoning capacity untapped.

Proposed Method: We introduce Coverage-Guided RLVR (CG-RLVR), which augments standard verifiable correctness rewards with a diversity bonus that incentivizes the model to produce structurally distinct correct solutions. Concretely, we maintain a rolling solution archive per problem and reward trajectories proportionally to their edit-distance (or embedding-distance) from archived solutions. This encourages exploration of the base model's full solution manifold. Additionally, we propose a 'coverage curriculum' that progressively raises the k threshold used during training, explicitly targeting high-k coverage as a training objective rather than just evaluation metric.

Experiments: (1) Compare pass@k curves (k=1 to 256) of CG-RLVR vs. standard GRPO/PPO/REINFORCE on MATH500, AIME, and LiveCodeBench; (2) Measure whether CG-RLVR closes the gap between RLVR and base model pass@k ceilings; (3) Perplexity and solution-cluster analyses to verify emergence of reasoning patterns absent in base model; (4) Ablate diversity reward weight and archive update strategies across Qwen2.5-Math and DeepSeek-R1-Distill families.

title: Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping: Expanding Base Model Reasoning Boundaries via Diversity-Incentivized RLVR
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR training merely reshapes the output distribution of base models without expanding their underlying reasoning coverage—base models at large k already cover solutions that RLVR discovers. This implies RLVR's reward signal inadvertently collapses solution diversity rather than exploring genuinely novel reasoning paths. Proposed Method: We introduce Coverage-Guided RLVR (CG-RLVR), which augments standard verifiable-reward RL with an explicit diversity bonus that incentivizes the model to generate reasoning trajectories not already well-represented in its base model distribution. Specifically, we compute trajectory novelty as inverse perplexity under the frozen base model, weighted by a diversity coefficient that decays as coverage saturates. We combine this intrinsic diversity reward with the extrinsic correctness reward, pushing the policy to explore low-probability but correct reasoning chains. We additionally incorporate a distillation warm-start from a stronger teacher to seed diverse reasoning patterns before RL fine-tuning. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH500, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and GeoQA using pass@k (k up to 256) as the primary metric, alongside coverage and perplexity analyses from the anchor paper. Ablations examine diversity coefficient scheduling, teacher model strength, and interaction with different RL algorithms (PPO, GRPO, REINFORCE). We hypothesize CG-RLVR will measurably expand pass@k coverage beyond the base model upper bound identified in the anchor paper.

title: Coverage-Guided Exploration Bonuses for RLVR: Escaping the Base Model Reasoning Boundary
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR-trained LLMs fail to generate reasoning patterns not already present in the base model—RLVR essentially selects and amplifies existing capabilities rather than discovering new ones. This fundamental limitation means reasoning coverage is bounded by the base model's latent distribution. Proposed Method: We introduce Coverage-Guided RLVR (CG-RLVR), which augments the reward signal with an intrinsic exploration bonus that explicitly incentivizes generation of reasoning trajectories underrepresented in the base model. We maintain a trajectory embedding store tracking the semantic diversity of reasoning chains produced so far. The exploration bonus is computed as the distance of a new reasoning trajectory from the base model's high-probability manifold (estimated via perplexity and embedding novelty against a reference corpus). This bonus is annealed during training to avoid reward hacking while consistently pushing the model to explore lower-probability but potentially valid reasoning paths. We further add a distillation warm-start phase using a stronger teacher to seed the trajectory store with genuinely novel patterns before RL begins. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH500, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning benchmarks using pass@k (k=1,16,64,256) and coverage metrics. We compare against standard GRPO, PPO, and distillation baselines, measuring whether CG-RLVR shrinks the gap between small-k and large-k performance—the key diagnostic from the anchor paper.

title: Escape Velocity: Measuring and Inducing Out-of-Distribution Reasoning in LLMs via Adversarial Environment Curricula
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR-trained models are bounded by base model coverage—they never produce reasoning patterns absent from the base. This suggests current RL training stays within the base model's support. We ask: can carefully designed adversarial problem curricula force RL to generate genuinely novel reasoning traces that escape base model coverage? Method: We introduce 'reasoning escape velocity' (REV), a metric quantifying how often an RL-trained model solves problems where the base model achieves zero coverage at any k. We construct an adversarial curriculum generator that iteratively identifies such 'dead zones'—problems where base model pass@k≈0 for k up to 256—and concentrates RL training there. We combine this with a diversity-seeking exploration bonus that penalizes solutions similar to base model generations, using embedding-space novelty rewards. We further investigate whether multi-turn tool-augmented interaction (code execution, symbolic solvers) enables reasoning steps genuinely absent from base model pretraining data. Experiments: We evaluate REV across Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3 families on competition mathematics (AIME, AMC), novel algorithmic puzzles, and out-of-distribution proof tasks. We compare against standard GRPO, distillation, and our adversarial curriculum, measuring pass@k coverage, token-level novelty relative to base model vocabulary distributions, and generalization to unseen problem structures.

title: Escape Velocity: Measuring and Inducing Genuine Reasoning Novelty in LLMs via Adversarial Boundary Probing
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR doesn't expand the base model's reasoning coverage beyond large-k pass@k limits, but it leaves open *why* this ceiling exists and *how* to break it. We hypothesize that RLVR fails to produce novel reasoning because reward signals remain within the distribution of problems the base model already partially solves — essentially polishing existing pathways rather than forging new ones. Proposed Method: We introduce 'Reasoning Novelty Score' (RNS), a metric quantifying how many correct solutions in a fine-tuned model fall outside the base model's reachable solution manifold (approximated via embedding-space clustering of correct reasoning traces at large k). We then design an adversarial curriculum: at each RL training step, we identify problem subsets where the base model has near-zero coverage (hard boundary problems), and upweight these in the reward signal. Additionally, we experiment with 'novelty bonuses' — extra rewards for solutions whose reasoning traces are far (in embedding space) from any base-model-generated trace. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, AIME, CodeForces, and a new visual geometry benchmark across Qwen-2.5, LLaMA-3, and DeepSeek-R1 base models, comparing standard GRPO/PPO, our adversarial curriculum, and distillation baselines using pass@k (k up to 256) and RNS. We expect adversarial curriculum + novelty bonuses to measurably increase RNS and push coverage beyond base-model limits.

title: Capability Injection via Targeted Distillation-RL Hybrid: Expanding Base Model Reasoning Boundaries Before RLVR Fine-tuning
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR is bounded by base model capabilities, while distillation can genuinely expand reasoning boundaries. This raises a critical question: can we design a hybrid training paradigm that first uses distillation to inject genuinely novel reasoning patterns, then applies RLVR to efficiently select and refine those patterns—achieving synergy beyond either approach alone? Proposed Method: We introduce a two-stage 'Distill-then-Reinforce' pipeline. Stage 1 performs targeted capability injection: identify specific reasoning sub-skills where the base model has near-zero pass@k coverage (e.g., combinatorial proofs, multi-step geometric reasoning), then distill from a stronger teacher model only on those skill-specific sub-distributions to expand the base model's coverage ceiling. Stage 2 applies RLVR starting from this distillation-expanded base, hypothesizing that RLVR's efficiency advantage at small-k can now operate over a broader capability space. We introduce a 'capability frontier' metric tracking how each stage shifts the pass@k curve across k values. Experiments: Evaluate on MATH500, OlympiadBench, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning tasks across three model families (Qwen, LLaMA, Gemma). Compare pure RLVR, pure distillation, naive sequential combination, and our targeted hybrid. Ablate distillation data selection strategies (coverage-gap-based vs. random vs. difficulty-based) to identify what makes distillation injection most effective before RLVR.

title: Escaping the Base Model Ceiling: Curriculum-Guided Multi-Turn Environment Interaction for Novel Reasoning Acquisition in LLMs
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR is bounded by base model coverage—it improves selection efficiency but cannot generate genuinely novel reasoning patterns. This ceiling problem fundamentally limits RL's potential for self-improvement in LLMs. We need methods that allow models to discover reasoning strategies absent in their base model's latent distribution. Proposed Method: We design a curriculum-guided multi-turn agent-environment interaction framework where the LLM iteratively explores structured reasoning environments (symbolic math solvers, code interpreters, proof assistants) that provide granular intermediate feedback beyond final answer correctness. Unlike standard RLVR, the environment exposes intermediate computational steps the model hasn't encountered, acting as an external knowledge scaffold. We combine this with a 'novelty bonus' reward that explicitly incentivizes reasoning trajectories with low base-model likelihood, measured via perplexity thresholding, pushing the model beyond its prior distribution. The curriculum progressively increases problem complexity to ensure stable learning. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, AIME, CodeContests, and a new geometric proof benchmark. Using pass@k (large k) as the primary metric—motivated directly by the anchor paper—we measure whether our approach genuinely expands coverage beyond the base model. We compare against six RLVR baselines and distillation, conducting ablations on novelty bonus weighting and curriculum design.

title: Reasoning Boundary Expansion via Iterative Distillation-RL Hybrid: Teaching Models to Exceed Their Own Coverage
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR cannot exceed base model reasoning coverage (pass@k ceiling), while distillation genuinely expands capabilities by introducing teacher knowledge. This raises a critical question: can we design a hybrid pipeline that first uses distillation to expand coverage boundaries, then applies RLVR to efficiently exploit the newly expanded space, creating a virtuous cycle that progressively pushes reasoning frontiers? Method: We propose Iterative Distillation-RL (IDRL), a staged training paradigm. In each cycle: (1) a stronger teacher (or ensemble of RLVR-trained peer models) distills novel reasoning patterns into the student via coverage-maximizing data selection—specifically targeting problems where the student's pass@k is low but teacher's is high; (2) RLVR fine-tunes the expanded model to improve pass@1 on the newly covered problems; (3) the updated model becomes the next cycle's weak teacher for harder problems. We use pass@k curves across k values as the primary diagnostic, tracking whether each distillation stage genuinely shifts the coverage ceiling. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH500, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and OlympiadBench across 3 model families (Qwen, DeepSeek, LLaMA), measuring per-cycle coverage expansion, pass@1 improvement, and generalization to held-out difficulty tiers. Ablations isolate distillation vs. RL contributions per cycle.

title: Boundary-Aware RLVR: Dynamically Estimating and Pushing Base Model Coverage Limits During Reinforcement Learning
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR merely reshapes sampling distributions within base model coverage rather than expanding it. A key open question is whether we can detect, in real-time during training, when RL is approaching the base model's coverage boundary—and whether targeted interventions at those boundaries can genuinely expand reasoning capacity. Proposed Method: We introduce Boundary-Aware RLVR (BA-RLVR), which maintains a running estimate of base model coverage by tracking pass@k curves (approximated via lightweight Monte Carlo sampling) for a sentinel problem set throughout training. When the coverage gap between RLVR-trained and base models shrinks below a threshold (indicating boundary proximity), we trigger a targeted distillation micro-phase: injecting teacher-generated solutions that lie outside current base model coverage (verified by near-zero base model pass@k), followed by RL fine-tuning on those newly absorbed patterns. This creates a curriculum that alternates between RL exploitation within known coverage and distillation-driven boundary expansion. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH500, AMC/AIME, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning (MathVista) using pass@k (k=1,8,64,256) as primary metric. Ablations compare: vanilla RLVR, distillation-only, BA-RLVR with various trigger thresholds, and oracle upper bounds. We measure genuine coverage expansion via perplexity divergence of solved problems from base model distribution.

title: Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping: Expanding RLVR's Reasoning Frontier Beyond Base Model Boundaries
description: Problem: As shown in the anchor paper, RLVR algorithms fail to elicit genuinely novel reasoning patterns beyond those latent in the base model—they essentially improve sampling efficiency (low pass@k) without expanding coverage (high pass@k). The base model already 'knows' the solutions but RLVR doesn't help discover new ones. Proposed Method: We introduce Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping (CGRS), which explicitly incentivizes exploration of reasoning paths not already accessible to the base model. Concretely, we maintain a trajectory diversity buffer tracking solution sketches (abstracted reasoning chains via clustering of intermediate steps). The RL reward is augmented with a novelty bonus inversely proportional to the cosine similarity between new trajectories and buffered base-model solutions, combined with a verifiable correctness reward. We additionally incorporate a curriculum that gradually increases problem difficulty to force the model beyond its current coverage boundary. Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate pass@k for k∈{1,4,16,64,256} on MATH, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning benchmarks comparing CGRS against standard RLVR baselines; (2) Measure coverage expansion relative to base model using the same perplexity/coverage framework from the anchor paper; (3) Ablate novelty bonus weight, buffer size, and curriculum schedule; (4) Analyze whether novel trajectories generalize to out-of-distribution problems, validating genuine reasoning capability expansion rather than redistribution.

title: Escaping the Base Model Ceiling: Curriculum-Driven Multi-Turn Environment Interaction for Genuinely Novel Reasoning in LLMs
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR merely reshapes sampling distributions within the base model's existing reasoning coverage rather than discovering genuinely novel reasoning patterns. This ceiling effect is particularly acute for hard problems that lie outside the base model's support. Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum-Driven Exploratory RL (CDERL), which combines two mechanisms to push beyond the base model ceiling: (1) a dynamic difficulty curriculum that progressively presents problems requiring reasoning chains NOT present in the base model's high-probability regions, identified via perplexity-based difficulty scoring; and (2) a multi-turn agent-environment interaction loop where the model can query external symbolic solvers, code interpreters, or retrieval tools mid-reasoning, creating opportunities to internalize genuinely new reasoning patterns through tool-augmented trajectories. The reward signal combines solution correctness with a novelty bonus measuring how much the generated reasoning chain diverges from the base model's top-k completions. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) competition-level math (AIME 2024-2025), (2) hard competitive programming (Codeforces div1/div2), and (3) novel logical reasoning benchmarks. Primary metrics are pass@k curves across varying k, coverage analysis against base model outputs, and perplexity of successful traces under the base model, directly addressing the anchor paper's diagnostic framework to measure whether our approach genuinely expands reasoning coverage.

title: Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping: Expanding Base Model Reasoning Boundaries via Diversity-Incentivized RLVR
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR merely selects from reasoning patterns already present in the base model rather than generating novel ones, with pass@k for large k being the key diagnostic. This reveals a fundamental limitation: current reward signals only incentivize correctness, not diversity or exploration of the base model's full solution space. Proposed Method: We introduce Coverage-Guided RLVR (CG-RLVR), which augments the standard verifiable reward with an explicit coverage bonus that incentivizes the model to produce solutions structurally dissimilar from previously generated correct trajectories. Concretely, we maintain a rolling buffer of correct solution embeddings per problem and compute a novelty score (via embedding distance clustering) as an additive reward term. This pushes the policy to explore underrepresented but valid reasoning paths in the base model's latent space, rather than collapsing onto high-probability correct solutions. We also experiment with temperature-annealing curricula that start with diverse high-temperature exploration and gradually sharpen. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH500, AIME, and HumanEval using pass@k (k up to 256) as primary metric, comparing against GRPO, PPO, and distillation baselines across Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3 model families. We measure whether CG-RLVR closes the gap between RLVR pass@k and base model pass@k, and conduct perplexity/coverage analyses to verify genuinely novel solution patterns emerge.

title: Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping: Expanding RLVR's Reasoning Frontier Beyond Base Model Boundaries
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR merely reshapes the sampling distribution of the base model rather than discovering genuinely new reasoning patterns, as evidenced by base models achieving higher pass@k at large k. This implies RLVR's reward signal is blind to novel reasoning trajectories already latent in the base model but rarely sampled. Proposed Method: We introduce Coverage-Guided RLVR (CG-RLVR), which explicitly incentivizes exploration of reasoning diversity. During training, we maintain a trajectory memory bank storing solution sketches (abstracted reasoning chains via clustering over chain-of-thought embeddings). The reward function is augmented with a novelty bonus: solutions that occupy underrepresented regions of reasoning space receive additional reward proportional to their distance from existing clusters. Concurrently, we use targeted temperature annealing—periodically spiking sampling temperature to probe low-probability reasoning paths, then fine-tuning on successful novel trajectories. This directly addresses the coverage gap identified in the anchor work. Experiments: (1) Compare pass@k (k=1 to 256) curves of CG-RLVR vs. standard RLVR and base models on MATH, AIME, and HumanEval; (2) Measure reasoning coverage via embedding cluster entropy; (3) Ablate novelty bonus weight and temperature schedule; (4) Test whether CG-RLVR produces reasoning patterns absent from the base model's top-1000 samples, using perplexity analysis from the anchor paper's methodology.

title: Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping: Expanding the Reasoning Frontier Beyond Base Model Boundaries in RLVR
description:
Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR only reshuffles probability mass within the base model's existing solution coverage rather than generating genuinely novel reasoning patterns. This means RLVR is fundamentally limited by base model coverage at large k. The key question is: can we design RL training objectives that explicitly pressure the model to discover solutions outside the base model's support?

Proposed Method: We introduce Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping (CGRS), which augments standard RLVR with a novelty bonus that rewards the RL-trained model for generating correct solutions that the base model assigns low probability. Specifically, for each verified-correct rollout, we compute a novelty score as the negative log-likelihood under the frozen base model, and add this as a weighted auxiliary reward alongside the verifiable correctness signal. This creates explicit pressure to explore low-probability-under-base reasoning chains. To prevent degenerate solutions, we additionally employ a semantic diversity constraint via clustering of solution embeddings within each training batch.

Experiments: (1) Evaluate pass@k for k up to 256 on MATH, AIME, and LiveCodeBench, comparing CGRS against standard GRPO/PPO and distillation baselines across Qwen2.5-Math and DeepSeek-R1 model families. (2) Measure base-model coverage expansion quantitatively using the anchor paper's perplexity and coverage metrics. (3) Ablate novelty bonus weight and diversity constraint strength. (4) Analyze whether expanded coverage corresponds to structurally distinct proof strategies via manual annotation.

title: Breaking the Base Model Ceiling: Curriculum-Guided Multi-Turn Environment Interaction for Genuinely Novel Reasoning in LLMs
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR is bounded by the base model's existing reasoning patterns—it improves selection (pass@1) but not coverage (pass@k). This ceiling suggests current single-turn, outcome-reward RL cannot elicit genuinely new capabilities. We hypothesize that iterative, multi-turn agent-environment interaction with carefully structured curriculum can force the model into reasoning regimes absent from its base distribution. Method: We propose Curriculum-Guided Exploratory RLVR (CGE-RLVR), combining: (1) a difficulty-aware curriculum that progressively introduces problems requiring reasoning chains provably absent from base model samples (verified via embedding-space novelty detection); (2) multi-turn scaffolded environments where the model receives intermediate verification feedback—subgoal checks, counterexamples, and partial credit—rather than only terminal rewards; (3) an explicit diversity bonus that penalizes reasoning paths with high cosine similarity to base model generations. Experiments: We evaluate on math (MATH-500, AIME), code synthesis (LiveCodeBench), and scientific reasoning (GPQA), measuring pass@k for k∈{1,4,16,64,256} alongside embedding-space coverage metrics. We compare against standard GRPO, distillation baselines, and ablations of each CGE-RLVR component. Success criterion: CGE-RLVR trained models must surpass base model pass@k at large k, demonstrating genuine reasoning expansion beyond the base model ceiling identified in the anchor paper.

title: Reasoning Boundary Expansion via Hybrid Distillation-RL: Combining Teacher Knowledge with Verifiable Reward Signals
description:
Problem: The anchor paper reveals that RLVR is bounded by base model reasoning coverage, while distillation genuinely expands capabilities but lacks the optimization pressure of verifiable rewards. This creates a fundamental gap: can we combine distillation's ability to introduce novel reasoning patterns with RLVR's selective reinforcement of correct solutions?

Proposed Method: We propose a staged hybrid training paradigm called DistRL. First, perform targeted distillation from a stronger teacher model specifically on problems where the base model has zero pass@k coverage, injecting novel reasoning patterns. Second, apply RLVR on the distillation-augmented model to consolidate and refine these new capabilities. We introduce a 'novelty-weighted' reward that upweights problems where distillation expanded coverage beyond the original base model, encouraging RL to exploit newly introduced reasoning patterns rather than just refining existing ones. A KL-divergence regularizer prevents collapse back to base model behavior.

Experiments: (1) Compare DistRL against pure RLVR, pure distillation, and naive distillation+RLVR baselines on MATH, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning benchmarks; (2) Measure pass@k at varying k to track genuine coverage expansion; (3) Ablate the novelty-weighted reward and staging order; (4) Analyze whether DistRL's gains persist under distribution shift to unseen problem types. Success metric: DistRL should exceed teacher's pass@1 on held-out hard problems while outperforming pure distillation at large k.

title: Breaking the Base Model Ceiling: Curriculum-Driven Multi-Turn Environment Interaction for Novel Reasoning Acquisition in LLMs
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR-trained models are bounded by their base model's reasoning coverage—they improve pass@1 but never exceed base model pass@k at large k, suggesting no genuinely new reasoning patterns emerge. This ceiling effect limits RL's potential for true capability expansion. Proposed Method: We design a multi-turn agent-environment interaction framework where the LLM iteratively refines solutions through structured external feedback loops (compiler outputs, proof checkers, numerical simulators), combined with a curriculum that deliberately targets problems outside the base model's high-probability generation mass. Specifically, we identify 'capability gaps'—problems where base model pass@256 < 10%—and construct a progressive curriculum using difficulty-aware problem synthesis. We augment RLVR with a diversity bonus that penalizes solutions similar to those the base model generates with high probability, explicitly incentivizing exploration of novel reasoning paths. Planned Experiments: (1) Measure pass@k (k up to 256) before/after training on gap problems across Qwen2.5-Math and DeepSeek-R1 families; (2) Track coverage expansion over training via embedding-space novelty metrics; (3) Compare against standard RLVR and distillation baselines on MATH500, AIME, and Lean4 proof tasks; (4) Ablate multi-turn feedback depth vs. diversity bonus contributions to ceiling-breaking.

title: Escaping the Base Model Ceiling: Novelty-Driven Exploration in RLVR via Diversity Bonuses
description: Problem: The anchor paper reveals that RLVR-trained LLMs fail to generate reasoning patterns beyond those latent in the base model, suggesting current reward signals only reinforce already-known solutions rather than incentivizing genuinely novel strategies. We hypothesize this is partly because standard RLVR uses correctness-only rewards, which exploit high-probability reasoning paths without encouraging exploration of lower-probability but valid alternatives. Proposed Method: We augment RLVR with a novelty-driven intrinsic reward that explicitly incentivizes reasoning diversity. Concretely, during training we maintain a rolling buffer of recent chain-of-thought trajectories and compute a novelty bonus based on n-gram dissimilarity and structural edit distance between newly generated reasoning paths and buffered ones. This bonus is added to the verifiable correctness reward, encouraging the policy to discover structurally distinct solution strategies. To prevent degenerate novelty (nonsensical chains), we add a perplexity penalty relative to the base model. Experiments: (1) Compare pass@k curves (large k) against standard RLVR baselines across math (MATH-500, AMC/AIME), coding (HumanEval), and visual reasoning benchmarks; (2) Measure coverage expansion over base model using the anchor paper's methodology; (3) Ablate novelty bonus weight and buffer size; (4) Qualitatively analyze whether discovered reasoning paths are genuinely novel vs. paraphrases. Success criterion: statistically significant improvement in pass@k at large k, closing the gap with base model coverage.

title: Reasoning Frontier Expansion via Iterative Distillation-RL Cycling: Breaking the Base Model Ceiling
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR is bounded by base model capabilities (coverage ceiling), while distillation genuinely expands reasoning patterns. This raises a critical question: can we iteratively break the ceiling by alternating distillation and RL phases, where each distillation step introduces new reasoning patterns from a stronger teacher, and each subsequent RL phase consolidates and refines them? Proposed Method: We introduce DIRLC (Distillation-RL Cycling), a training paradigm that alternates between (1) knowledge distillation from a stronger teacher model to inject novel reasoning trajectories beyond the current model's coverage, and (2) RLVR training to selectively amplify high-reward patterns from the expanded distribution. The key insight is using the post-distillation model as the new 'base' for RL, resetting the ceiling at each cycle. We track pass@k coverage across cycles to quantitatively measure ceiling expansion. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, AIME, LiveCodeBench, and visual reasoning benchmarks using 7B and 14B models. Ablations compare: single distillation, single RL, distillation-only cycling, RL-only cycling, and DIRLC. We measure pass@k for large k values, perplexity of generated solutions, and novel reasoning pattern emergence across cycles. We hypothesize that 3-4 cycles substantially expand the effective reasoning frontier beyond any single phase.

title: Curriculum-Guided Exploration Bonuses for RLVR: Pushing Beyond Base Model Coverage Boundaries
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR-trained LLMs fail to generate reasoning patterns not already present in the base model, with pass@k at large k revealing the base model as an upper bound on coverage. This suggests current RLVR training lacks mechanisms to explore genuinely novel solution strategies. Method: We propose Coverage-Driven Exploration RLVR (CDE-RLVR), which augments standard RLVR with intrinsic exploration bonuses that reward novel reasoning trajectories. Concretely, we maintain a trajectory embedding store and compute novelty scores (via kernel density estimation over solution embeddings) as auxiliary rewards. A curriculum scheduler progressively increases the novelty bonus weight as training advances, preventing reward hacking while encouraging exploration. We additionally incorporate deliberate perturbation of intermediate reasoning steps during rollout generation to escape local solution clusters identified by the base model. Experiments: We train Qwen2.5-Math and DeepSeek-R1-Distill variants with CDE-RLVR on MATH500, AIME, and LiveCodeBench, evaluating pass@k for k up to 256. Our primary metric is whether CDE-RLVR closes the coverage gap between RLVR models and base models identified in the anchor paper. We also measure whether novel trajectories discovered during training transfer to out-of-distribution benchmarks, and ablate novelty bonus design choices against distillation baselines.

title: Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping: Expanding RLVR Beyond Base Model Boundaries via Diversity-Aware Training
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that RLVR merely resharpens the base model's existing reasoning distribution (improving pass@1 while reducing pass@k coverage), rather than genuinely expanding reasoning capabilities. This suggests current reward signals optimize for exploitation over exploration of the reasoning space. Proposed Method: We introduce Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping (CGRS), which augments standard verifiable rewards with an explicit diversity bonus that incentivizes the model to generate reasoning trajectories dissimilar from its current policy's observed solutions. Concretely, we maintain a rolling buffer of successful solution embeddings and add a novelty reward term (based on cosine distance in reasoning-step embedding space) to the RL objective. This pushes the policy toward underexplored but correct reasoning paths. We additionally incorporate a 'boundary probing' curriculum that periodically evaluates pass@k coverage and upweights training problems where the model's coverage gap (relative to base model) is largest. Experiments: We train Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3 variants using GRPO+CGRS on MATH, AIME, and LiveCodeBench, evaluating pass@k for k∈{1,4,16,64,256}. We compare against standard GRPO, distillation baselines, and ablations removing each reward component. Success is measured by whether CGRS-trained models exceed base model pass@k at large k values, directly targeting the key failure mode identified in the anchor paper.

title: Coverage-Guided Reward Shaping: Expanding Reasoning Boundaries Beyond Base Model Ceilings in RLVR
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows RLVR merely selects from reasoning patterns already present in the base model (bounded by pass@k at large k), failing to generate genuinely novel capabilities. This ceiling effect means current RLVR approaches waste RL's exploratory potential. We propose a coverage-guided reward shaping mechanism that actively incentivizes exploration beyond the base model's existing solution distribution. Method: We maintain a dynamic solution fingerprint bank (using program traces, proof step embeddings, or chain-of-thought clustering) tracking which reasoning pathways the base model can already generate at high k. During RLVR training, we augment the standard correctness reward with a novelty bonus that rewards solutions whose reasoning trajectories fall outside this fingerprint bank, combined with a diversity penalty discouraging redundant within-batch solutions. We additionally incorporate a 'surprise' metric measuring solution perplexity relative to the frozen base model, rewarding low-probability-but-correct solutions. Experiments: We train Qwen2.5-Math and DeepSeek-R1 base models using GRPO with our augmented rewards on MATH500, AIME, and CodeContests. We evaluate using the anchor paper's pass@k framework (large k), coverage analysis, and a new 'expansion ratio' metric measuring fraction of correct solutions genuinely outside the base model's reachable set. Ablations isolate each reward component's contribution to coverage expansion versus accuracy tradeoffs.

title: Escape Velocity: Curriculum-Guided Multi-Turn Environment Interaction for Genuinely Novel Reasoning in LLMs
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that current RLVR methods merely surface pre-existing base model capabilities rather than generating genuinely new reasoning patterns. The paper suggests multi-turn agent-environment interaction as a promising direction, but this remains unexplored. We hypothesize that iterative, environment-grounded exploration with structured curriculum progression can push models beyond their base model coverage ceiling. Method: We propose CurriculumRL-Interact, a multi-turn RLVR framework where the LLM interacts with a symbolic reasoning environment (e.g., a Python interpreter or formal proof assistant) across sequential sub-steps. The curriculum dynamically selects problems just beyond the model's current pass@1 frontier, using a difficulty estimator based on base model perplexity. Crucially, intermediate environment feedback signals (partial credit, error traces) serve as dense rewards, enabling the model to develop reasoning chains unobservable in base model generation. A diversity bonus penalizes solutions already covered by the base model's pass@k distribution, explicitly incentivizing novel reasoning patterns. Experiments: We evaluate on MATH, AIME, CodeContests, and formal theorem proving (Lean 4), measuring (1) pass@k curves relative to base model ceilings, (2) solution coverage overlap with base model generations, (3) perplexity of novel correct solutions, and (4) ablations over curriculum aggressiveness and diversity bonuses.
